items.title: Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027
items.desc: Starting in 2027, Google plans to turn off AI features in its school products by default, letting schools decide what to enable. The catch: schools that block AI entirely on their devices will also lose access to Google Search, since the two systems are now too deeply intertwined to separate. Given Google's grip on the US school market, that "choice" doesn't leave schools with much room to maneuver. The article Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027 appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Starting in early 2027, Google will give schools an ultimatum: accept AI for students or lose access to Google Search entirely. Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will all be off by default for student accounts. Schools can turn each one on individually. But a version of search without AI? That's no longer on the table. The New York Times broke the story first. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, said search and AI have become too tightly fused to pull apart. Google recently flipped AI features on by default inside its learning platform Classroom for schools with Gemini access. That move drew backlash, and the company is now reversing course. Schools that choose to enable search will get two flavors: search with full AI overviews and AI chat, or search with "Guided Learning," a mode designed to steer students toward answers rather than hand them over directly. None of this happens in a vacuum. Google dominates the US school market with Chromebooks, Gmail, and Classroom. Education professor Morgan Polikoff called the move a textbook case of the tech industry shoving AI onto people whether they want it or not. The country's two largest school districts, New York City and Los Angeles, had already pulled back on AI for students in September. Los Angeles specifically wanted to keep using Google Search without AI overviews. Google won't let them. items.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
items.desc: Called FlashProve, the system would let anyone check that an AI response really came from the model it claims to be from.
items.full: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Image Credits: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images AI Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity Russell Brandom 2:41 PM PST · November 3, 2026 Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using. Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results. FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?” To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device. As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub . Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab. “This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . items.title: Re-Implementing :nth-child() With Modern CSS
items.desc: Combining :nth-child with style queries and sibling-index() to conditionally select child elements. Re-Implementing :nth-child() With Modern CSS originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full:
NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. The title sounds a bit strange, right? Why re-implement an existing feature, that’s completely useless! I have two reasons for that. The first reason is to be able to adjust the :nth-child() arguments on the fly. Let’s suppose you have the following: div:nth-child(5n + 8) { background: red; } And you decide to update the 5 or the 8 . The only way is to manually rewrite the selector, which isn’t ideal. We cannot have something like the below where you can change the variables as you want: .container { --A: 5; --B: 8; } .container > div:nth-child(var(--A)*n + var(--B)) { background: red; } With my implementation, you will be able to do it! The second reason is to have fun and play with some new features. You will probably never need to rely on a dynamic :nth-child() selector, but I am sure you will learn one or two useful tricks along the way. We will rely on the same code structure in all the examples: a container with a bunch of
elements inside it.
And the container controls the variables of :nth-child() : .container { --A: ; --B: ; } .container > div { /* based on the values of --A and --B change the background value */ background: ??; } I am not saying that this structure is mandatory for the implementation. I just considered a simple one to keep things easy to follow. :nth-child(B) Let’s start with the simplest case, a selector that selects only one element: div:nth-child(5) { } I don’t think I need to explain what this selector does. The 5 is nothing but the index of the selected element. So, if B is equal to the index of the element, that element is selected. We can translate this into the following CSS code: .container { --B: 5; } .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red); } Is this a valid CSS code?! Yes, it’s valid, and it works! I am using the new if() syntax that allows me to define a condition within style() . If that condition is true, the background color is set to red. Otherwise, nothing happens. We can also have an if/else : .container { --B: 5; } .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red; else: lightblue); } CodePen Embed Fallback The if() syntax is not that complex. In our case, we only have one condition, so you can see it as follows: .container div { background: if(style( condition ): ; else: ); } The tricky part is how to define the condition within style() . I wrote a small post explaining this part, so do yourself a favor and go read it before we continue: “The Hidden Trick of Style Queries and if() .” It’s a quick reading with crucial details that helps you better understand how if() works. From there, you will notice that our condition can be written several ways that are all valid: .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red); background: if(style(sibling-index() = var(--B)): red); background: if(style(var(--B) = sibling-index()): red); background: if(style(--B = sibling-index()): red); } We have our first implementation! items.title: How to implement AI search in WordPress and stay in control
items.desc: Imagine your agency manages the WordPress help center for an appointment-booking software company. Customers keep asking support how to reschedule recurring appointments. The instructions already exist, ...
items.full: Imagine your agency manages the WordPress help center for an appointment-booking software company. Customers keep asking support how to reschedule recurring appointments. The instructions already exist, but a search for “move my Friday bookings” doesn’t lead to the guide. The client wants to try AI search. Instead of relying on customers to type the exact words in an article, it could match their question to a guide with a similar meaning. The first version would return links to existing documentation. Choosing a provider raises a harder question. Will the service you recommend today still suit the site next year? You can’t promise that, and the client shouldn’t need that promise before you start. You can keep the original guides in WordPress and build the integration so replacing the search service doesn’t mean rebuilding the help center. This article follows that project from a limited trial to wider use. It explains which parts of the setup need to remain under your control and how hosting can give your team room to adjust no matter what AI tool, trends, or integration you opt for. Here’s one possible scenario. Your developer starts comparing services just as another vendor announces a new search product. The client forwards the announcement: “Should we wait for this?” Meanwhile, support keeps sending the same article link. Before buying anything, your agency can investigate why the current search misses the guide. It’s possible that the help center stores articles in a custom post type that the current search configuration leaves out. Or the article calls recurring appointments “series management,” a phrase customers rarely use. Those problems need different fixes, of course. Developers can check whether WordPress search includes the help-center articles, and an editor can add the wording customers use and clarify which instructions cover the current software version. Recent support tickets give you real questions to test. The support team already knows which guide answers each question, which is helpful. Trying out those questions on the site shows where search fails, without guessing what customers might type. Semantic search is another way to improve this. It uses machine learning to find content with a similar meaning to the query, even when the wording differs. This helps connect phrases like “move my Friday bookings” to other phrases like “reschedule recurring appointments.” The underlying documentation still matters. If two guides describe different versions of the booking software, the search service needs enough information to distinguish them. Your agency can resolve those content problems while the purchasing decision stays open. When you test AI search, you have a cleaner library and a set of questions to compare against. Canceling the search subscription shouldn’t remove a single guide from the client’s WordPress site. Editors continue working in WordPress. The search provider holds an indexed copy of the content that the integration sends it. That distinction matters when you plan a replacement. items.title: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex
items.desc: Replacing JavaScript with a modern CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about. Gabriel Shoyombo explores what happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, sharing practical guidance to help you keep complexity in check during migration.
items.full: About The Author Gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer. He specializes in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue, TailwindCSS, and BootStrap, with a track record of … More about Gabriel ↬ Weekly tips on front-end & UX . Trusted by 182,000+ folks. How To Measure UX and Design Impact with Vitaly Friedman Celebrating 10 million developers Design Patterns For AI Interfaces with Vitaly Friedman Make Your Design System Work, for Humans and Robots with Javier Cuello Design Patterns For AI Interfaces, 30 lessons + UX training Replacing JavaScript with a modern CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about. Gabriel Shoyombo explores what happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, sharing practical guidance to help you keep complexity in check during migration. Have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor? You replace ResizeObserver with a container query, the diff is mostly red, and everyone approves it before lunch. This was what it looked like before you made the change: See the Pen [demo (before PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVJq) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide . Then, a week later, a card on the dashboard has vanished. A heading has grown on tablets for no reason anyone can explain. The spacing inside a comment is off. See the Pen [demo (after PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/gbmBopp) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide . None of these bugs are in the few lines you wrote. All of them arrived with those few lines of CSS. In my last article on how CSS is growing smarter , I left a few questions hanging at the end, including: What happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, and how do we debug conditional styles without a clear view of what triggered them? This article is my attempt to answer these two questions. I think it’s worth saying clearly that I am not saying modern CSS is bad. What I am saying is that: A CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about if you don’t understand how it relates to existing code, be it CSS or JavaScript. Think of a new CSS feature as a new tenant moving into a shared apartment. The tenant may be quiet and tidy, but they still share a kitchen with everyone who already lives there. In that case, CSS is now roommates with JavaScript, the component’s layout, the CSS Cascade, and the browser’s rendering engine. The apartment’s stability depends less on the tenant and more on how they get along with one another. That gives us two different things to measure, and a diff only shows the first one: I am not the only one thinking about this. Image Credits: Apple AI Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing Sarah Perez 11:20 PM PST · November 2, 2026 Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is now rolling out into beta testing, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes. The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist. However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps. Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them. With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation. Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things. When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and the visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said. These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them. The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations. Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. items.full: ChatGPT can now create animated GIFs. The update is based on OpenAI's new Images 2.6 model and is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users on web, desktop, and mobile apps, The Verge reports. Users can generate a GIF from a text prompt or uploaded photo, then adjust animation speed or edit individual frames. As an example, OpenAI showed how the prompt "Can you make a gif of a cat dancing?" produces several slight variations of a character that are strung together flipbook-style into a GIF. The model's image consistency appears strong enough to keep the character recognizable across frames, while earlier models would likely have altered its look too much from one frame to the next for the trick to work. Beyond GIFs, Images 2.6 is also meant to speed up image generation overall. For developers, OpenAI is also releasing the API models GPT-Image-2.6 "Flare" for efficient and "Sunburst" for higher-quality image generation. Both model variants were first introduced with Image 2.5 . OpeneAI says users now generate well over four billion images per week via ChatGPT and the API, one billion more than in September.
